name: Ligurian
confidence_why: Ancient Ligurian is known only from names and glosses, and the sole accent claim, de Bernardo Stempel's (2006; with Arenas Esteban 2011) antepenultimate-or-initial accent inferred from forms like *Bérgioma under her Celtoligurian hypothesis, is a reconstruction that Falileyev (2011) rejects as violating historical phonetics, while Kretschmer (1905), Whatmough (1937) and Falileyev (2020) say nothing about stress, so no placement can be stated for the language.

catalog_quote: - montem Berigiemam, from a nominative *Bérgioma, i.e. *bhergh-yo-mā ‘the highest’ with West-Celtic epenthetic vowel in the second syllable and an equally archaic superlative suffix, the positive grade being preserved in BergiomHi and BergionGeM. ... It is therefore possible to recognize the change of unstressed yo to (y)e as a Celtic isogloss, and even to compare it with what happened later on in Goidelic ... The accusative receives in fact a very simple explanation if we assume dekantem to be just the outcome of ... ‘the tenth’ with Celto-Ligurian unaccented e < *yo ... a few more examples of the regional Celtic monophthongization of unaccented yo to e seems to concentrate in the territory of the Convenae

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (14 pp., text, Palaeohispanica 6: 45-58). Both halves of the stitched quote are there verbatim: p. 46 (§1) "- montem Berigiemam, from a nominative *Bérgioma, i.e. *bhergh-yo-mā 'the highest' with West-Celtic epenthetic vowel in the second syllable and an equally archaic superlative suffix, the positive grade being preserved in BergiomHi and BergionGeM." and p. 47 (end of §2) "It is therefore possible to recognize the change of unstressed yo to (y)e as a Celtic isogloss, and even to compare it with what happened later on in Goidelic". The [..] in the report spans the rest of p. 46 and most of p. 47; the locator "pp. 46-47" is right. Further accent word…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls in Ancient Ligurian. The only accent-related claim in the accessible literature is de Bernardo Stempel's reconstruction that the Ligurian onomastic change *yo > (y)e (Blustiemelo, Lebriemelum, Nitielium, Berigiema) affected UNACCENTED *-yo-, with the accent placed earlier in the word (her *Bérgioma). This is a hypothesised accent condition on a sound change in reconstructed names under her Celtic-Ligurian hypothesis, not a description of a stress system.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the language is known only from names and glosses.
new_statements.domain_note: Reconstructed proto-forms of place/tribal names transmitted in Latin texts (Sententia Minuciorum, CIL V 7749); no attested prosody, no word-vs-phrase domain applicable.
new_statements.identity_note: Ancient Ligurian (anci1248, xlg) is a fragmentarily attested pre-Roman language of Liguria/NW Italy known only from names, glosses and a few disputed inscriptions; some scholars (de Bernardo Stempel, Delamarre) treat the Indo-European layer as a Celtic ('Celto-Ligurian') dialect, others (Kretschmer, Falileyev, Mees) as a separate IE language. Not to be confused with modern Ligurian (Romance, ligu1248).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Ligurian has an empty rule; the only existing statement (de Bernardo Stempel 2006, pp. 46-47) gives 'unstressed *yo > (y)e' and a reconstructed *Bérgioma with initial accent, reading 'none found'. This 2011 paper by the same author makes the underlying accent claim explicit: an antepenultimate/initial-syllable pattern (α) for the Ligurian-area Celtic names, compatible with *Bérgioma and with the p. 129 isogloss 'unstressed *-yo- > -ye- as shown by the tribal name Nitielium and the oronym Berigiema'. It adds a placement where the catalog had none, so it refines rather than contradicts; but it is a reconstruction under the contested view that the Ligurian names are Celt…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Under the authors' Celtic reading of the Ligurian onomastic layer ('Celtoligurian'), the older Celtic accent pattern (α) is what the Ligurian-area names mostly reflect: accent on the antepenultimate syllable, i.e. the first syllable of two- and three-syllable words, with posttonic reduction of -yo-/-o-, monophthongization of posttonic falling diphthongs and epenthesis in posttonic r/l + consonant clusters. The later Gaulish-Brittonic pattern (β) puts the accent on the penult. This is a reconstruction from name forms, not a description of a recorded language.
new_statements.exceptions: In Italy as a whole, 'unlike the Iberian Peninsula, the penultimate accentuation is by far the best attested' (p. 127); the antepenultimate pattern is the one found 'mostly in the Ligurian area', and the material documenting it 'is not always very old'. The penultimate pattern is said to lengthen a single consonant after the stressed penult and to reduce/assimilate vowels in the initial, unstressed syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: The work does not treat 'Ligurian' as a separate language: it calls the onomastic layer of Strabo's Ligystike 'Celtoligurian' / 'Ligurian Celtic' (p. 129) and lists its Celtic isoglosses (bh > b, loss of p-, lenition, unstressed *-yo- > -ye-, o > u before labials, assibilation, palatal anticipation, epenthesis, suffixes -enko-/-asko-). The accent statement (pp. 126-127) is therefore about the Celtic names of the Ligurian area, i.e. the same corpus that Glottolog anci1248 covers, but classified as Celtic rather than unclassified. The Hispanic accent discussion (pp. 125-126) concerns Hispano-Celtic/Celtiberian, not Ligurian.

readall_conflicts: Within this work there is no internal disagreement, but the claim is a reconstruction that depends on de Bernardo Stempel's view that the Ligurian onomastic layer is an archaic Celtic dialect ('Celtoligurian'); our files already records that Falileyev 2011 (Voprosy Jazykoznanija 2011/3, p. 106) accepts the 'unstressed *yo > ye' change as Ligurian but explicitly rejects her *Bérgioma reconstruction as violating historical phonetics, and Falileyev 2020 and Kretschmer 1905 say nothing about accent. So the antepenultimate/initial rule rests on one scholar's Celtic interpretation of name forms; no source opened describes the accent of Ancient Ligurian as a language in its own right, and the paper itself notes that in Italy the penultimate (Gaulish) pattern is 'by far the best attested' and that the Ligurian-area material is 'not always very old'.

sources.locator: pp. 46-47 (§1 '*yo > ye in Ligurian onomastics', §2 'The Celto-Ligurian dialect'); cf. p. 49
sources.note: §1-2 (pp. 45-47): the recurrent Ligurian onomastic change *yo > (y)e (Devoto, Lejeune) is framed as 'the change of unstressed yo to (y)e' and treated as a Celtic isogloss; montem Berigiemam is reconstructed as *Bérgioma with an initial accent mark (p. 46); p. 49: 'Celto-Ligurian unaccented e < *yo'. This is an accent condition assumed for a reconstructed sound change in names under a Celtic hypothesis, not a description of where stress falls in the language.

sources.citation: Falileyev, Alexander. 2020. "The Silent Europe." Palaeohispanica 20: 887-919. DOI 10.36707/palaeohispanica.v0i20.372
sources.note: Section 2 (pp. 891-895) surveys the 'Ligurian' onomastic complex and on p. 895 summarises the historical phonetics of Indo-European Ligurian (centum; *bh > b, deaspiration; initial *p- and sonorants. most vowels kept, *o sporadically; *u > o in some positions; *yo > ye; suffixes -ink-, -isk-, -l-, -jo-, -ask-). Nothing on accent or stress; the only 'stress' hits are the verb 'stressed' in citations.
